issue_context.title: [API Proposal]: `System.Linq.Shuffle()`
comments:
See  https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/78419#issuecomment-1315891664, https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/73864#issuecomment-1315849980.

`Shuffle` depends highly on the random algorithm instead of `IEnumerable<T>`. At least it's easy to add an extension for yourself.

Even if you say "you can easily implement it yourself," it is not efficient, and if someone (including me) has implemented it themselves many times, I think that is a reason to include it in the official API.
`OrderBy()` is not the optimal implementation, nor is it the optimal use. It is for "sorting".

I don't think it's a problem even if `Random.Shuffle()` is used internally.
(Strictly speaking, an inside-out implementation would be more efficient than the method of "copying to an internal array and then performing an inplace shuffle".)
Even though `Random.Shuffle()` exists, additional implementation is currently required to support `IEnumerable<T>`. (It will probably be necessary to make it `T[]` first.)
Therefore, I think there is a reason for its existence.

If "Random, not the collection, should be responsible", would that be `Random.Shared.Shuffle(IEnumerable<T> source)`?
Still, I personally prefer the LINQ style.
How could this be implemented without bias in cases where the length of the enumerable isn't known ahead of time or could potentially be infinite?

To answer my own question, this is typically addressed using [reservoir sampling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reservoir_sampling). This necessarily introduces bias in the generated permutations, however it might be a good-enough compromise for some use cases.

One potential implementation could involve implementing the classical shuffling algorithm for sources implementing `IList<T>`/`IReadOnlyList<T>` and then falling back to reservoir sampling for everything else. The problem with such an approach is that it violates LSP, two enumerables with identical elements would be shuffled using different algorithms with different statistical properties depending on what other interfaces they happen to implement.

As far as I understand, reservoir sampling is an algorithm that extracts elements partially, so it may be difficult to apply it to the current application, which requires shuffling the entire array.
In addition, the result cannot be determined until all elements are enumerated (at least once), so I don't think it can handle infinitely long `IEnumerable<T>`.
(I'm sorry if I'm wrong, please point it out.)

In my opinion, it would be implemented like `Reverse()` does now, by first materializing the array with `ToArray()`, then shuffling it, and returning it in order.
`OrderBy()` seems to have a separate array of the original data obtained with `ToArray()` and a sorted index.

Of course, there may be better ideas.

> In my opinion, it would be implemented like Reverse() does now, by first materializing the array with ToArray(), then shuffling it, and returning it in order.

That is my expectation as well. It would do the simple/obvious thing, basically:
```C#
T[] data = source.ToArray();
Random.Shared.Shuffle(data);
```

Which begs the question how much value adding this actually provides.

> Which begs the question how much value adding this actually provides.

The only benefit I can think of is avoiding copying when the source is a list.

> > Which begs the question how much value adding this actually provides.
> 
> The only benefit I can think of is avoiding copying when the source is a list.

That would violate expectations set by other LINQ APIs like Order, OrderBy, Reverse, Except, Intersect, etc.
In what way?

> In what way?

Maybe I misunderstood your suggestion, which I thought was to mutate the source rather than copying.

That said, it would still deviate from Reverse, for example, which snapshots the contents when calling GetEnumerator, such that changes to the source after that aren't reflected in the reversed data. There's a long-standing debate about that behavior, though.

> > In what way?
> 
> Maybe I misunderstood your suggestion, which I thought was to mutate the source rather than copying.

My thinking was that we could replicate the permutation algorithm for `IList<T>` using an iterator. It should make it more efficient to sample data by doing `list.Shuffle().Take(10)` when `list` is sufficiently large.

> That said, it would still deviate from Reverse

I can see how changing `Reverse` might be a point of contention, but I don't think he have to replicate that behavior for a new method.

> It should make it more efficient to sample data by doing list.Shuffle().Take(10) when list is sufficiently large.

Sure, if we believe that to be a common case, it could be optimized in combination with subsequent operations _if_ the source is of a known length.
I think it might be worth discussing this in API review.

Note to implementer (@eiriktsarpalis?) - please make sure the docs explicitly state whether a CSPRNG is used. (Basically, just state whether the shuffle is "strongly" random from a cryptographic sense.)

review_comments:
It's so special if `takeCount` is `1` so that the list allocated here (even though the capacity has been set) might be removed in theory. The cost is a `bool` branch and more code lines.

I don't know how to judge the balance 🤣 . It seems that randomly picking a single element is more often than other count numbers.

> It seems that randomly picking a single element is more often than other count numbers.

How so?

I do not think it's worth spending even more code optimizing that case until it's proven to really be necessary. It would non-trivially complicate things, all to avoid an extra allocation, when we're already allocating for the Shuffle enumerable and the Take enumerable and whatever the input to the Shuffle was.

> until it's proven to really be necessary

Got it.

>  It seems that randomly picking a single element is more often than other count numbers.

Do you mean `list.Shuffle().First()`? It will call `ShuffleIterator.TryGetFirst`, which has been optimized.

Is it worth asserting that first.Distinct().Count() is also equal to the requested count?  That is, that none of "too short", "too long", (or, elsewhere "just right") has a path that duplicates entries?

(By which I mean that it doesn't double-dip an index.  Which this test is showing since all elements were distinct before it started)

Should we also add a bespoke implementation targeting `IList<T>` directly? Seems like a win from a performance perspective. It would involve re-implementing the permutation algorithm but it's trivial and we already do this for the AsyncEnumerable case.

> Should we also add a bespoke implementation targeting IList<T> directly?

What would it do differently?

Do you mean avoiding copying the source entirely and just yielding elements directly from the underlying collection? How would you reimplement the permutation algorithm to avoid needing to allocate, or would you instead be doing what OrderBy does and allocate an int[] with the positions, and hope that int is smaller than T?

It would make Skip/Take easier, though.
Not necessarily certain if this is going to be faster compared to just doing `.ToArray()` though..

I'm a little hesitant to use ArrayPool like that in an iterator across enumeration; it means leaking a buffer if the enumerator isn't disposed, for example. Do we use ArrayPool like that anywhere else in enumeration in LINQ? I thought we only used it in ToArray/ToList/etc.

In hindsight I think it's fine to keep `ToArray` for everything. I was hoping I could pin this down to a simpler solution, but I couldn't find anything not forcing either $O(n)$ space, additional iterations through the collection like above, or $O(n^2)$ time.
Hopefully this went into your analyzer notes for patterns to match against
My understanding is that builds of System.Linq that have this optimization enabled will behave differently when calling `Shuffle().Take()` on infinite enumerables. Are we ok with this?
Correspondingly `infiniteEnumerable.Shuffle().Take(1).Count()` completes whereas `await infiniteEnumerable.AsAsyncEnumerable().Shuffle().Take(1).CountAsync()` diverges.

We've now shifted away from two different builds and instead just have a single build with a feature switch, so it's really a question of whether the feature switch impacts behavior, and that's much more palatable, since that's what feature switches are for :)

This whole file doesn't come into play if the size-optimized feature switch is set, so I'm not sure there's much we can do about it, unless you're suggesting blocking enumerables > 2^31 elements from working even when we can support them?
Not a huge deal, but couldn't this be expressed as an extension method we polyfill?

Not until we have extension properties and extension statics.

A real polyfill for it would also be much more code, as the instance returned by Shared is usable from any thread, not just the current one.
Is it possible to deal with a specific case `Shuffle().Take(1)`? When randomly picking one element only, shuffling all elements seems to be a waste.

It's possible, but it requires either adding another separate iterator impl or adding the additional take count to this one and factoring it into all the implementations. It's also much more complicated for counts larger than 1. That's all why I skipped it initially.

> That's all why I skipped it initially.

Got it. I think `Shuffle().Take(N)` will become a relatively hot requirement after releasing this API. It is indeed a performance detail if a separate iterator(`TakeShuffleIterator<TSource>`) can reduce the element swap times with `O(N)` instead of `O(Length)`. I see your another commit adding it. That's wonderful 👍 !
@stephentoub not sure if TryGetLast is impl correctly here?
It is. This is a shuffle, so the index doesn't matter; last is logically the same as first.
Didn't see it that way, but indeed, the index doesn't really matter. Thanks!
So `Shuffle` will always call `source.ToArray` to allocate an array, and never change the source elements' positions. Would it be better add some remarks in the API doc?
This is how all LINQ methods work.
